Acrylic paint-along · beginner

A striped hot air balloon floating over a lavender field at sunset, with purple mountains, a golden hill, and one big tree.

Start on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

12 stepsFocal point: The striped balloon at the upper left (envelope from 20% to 36% across, 3% to 27% down). Light: The setting sun, low in the middle of the picture (43% across, 41% down). Cloud edges facing the sun glow gold, the tree is lit on its left side, and the lavender tops catch pink-lilac light.How this lesson was made

What you need

Tubes

  • Titanium white
  • Cadmium yellow medium (hue)
  • Cadmium red medium (hue)
  • Ultramarine blue
  • Burnt sienna

Brushes

  • 1 inch flat: covering and blending the whole skyFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • #10 round: the cloud masses and low streaksRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #8 round: dry brushing the orange and gold on the cloud undersidesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • #6 round: dabbing the sun diskRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • 1/2 inch flat: cutting the ridge lines and filling the mountainsFlat: square end, for big areas and straight edges
  • old stiff flat or #8 round: tapping the bushesOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • #4 round: the trunk and branchesRound: pointed tip, thin or thick depending on how hard you press
  • old stiff flat: tapping the leaf clustersOld stiff flat: worn, splayed bristles, for rough texture like grass and foliage
  • Liner (#1 or #0): the ropesLiner: long, very thin bristles, for fine lines like twigs and grass

Also

  • White canvas or canvas board
  • Water jar and paper towel
  • Palette or paper plate for mixing

The steps

Step 1Step 2Step 3Step 4Step 5Step 6Step 7Step 8Step 9Step 10Step 11Step 12

STEP 1 OF 12

Blend the sunset sky

  1. The light comes from the sun, low and a little left of center. Keep every highlight on the side facing it.
  2. With the 1 inch flat and creamy Sky blue, paint long side-to-side strokes across the top tenth.
  3. X-stroke Sunset orange from the blue down to a straight line about 63% down, past where the hills go.
  4. While wet, X-stroke Glow gold into a bright patch a little left of center, just under halfway down. Smooth each join with light, long strokes; stop when it drags.
  5. Done: blue top, orange middle, golden glow, white canvas below the line.
Paints for this step3 paints, 3 new
  • Sky blue new3 parts white, 2 parts ultramarine
  • Sunset orange new3 parts yellow, 2 parts red
  • Glow gold new3 parts yellow, 1 part red

Colors dry a little darker: dab each mix on the palette's edge and let it dry before painting a big area.

Mix plenty of Sunset orange; the sky is a big area.

Brushes

1 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Pull the flat side to side across the canvas in long, even strokes for the blue band at the top.

X stroke. Criss-cross the flat in overlapping X shapes to lay in and blend the orange and gold; then go over it with light, long strokes to smooth it.

Watch out: Don't stop the orange at the mountain line: run it down to the straight line so the hills go over it.

Watch out: Don't keep blending once it drags; streaks are fine, and it will dry.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

How this picture was made Render · 1 try · $0.031

Why this step, now: Every later layer sits on the sky, and it's one wet blend, so it goes first and runs well past the horizon.

Why this tool: The step is the finish with everything in front of the sky removed. No composite tool exists yet, and the clouds, balloon, and tree hide sky that no filter could invent.

No diagram: A blended gradient; the words give where each color goes.

STEP 2 OF 12

Block in the cloud shapes

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the #10 round and creamy Cloud coral, scrub small circles for a big cloud top right: from 42% across to the right edge, top edge down to 28%.
  3. Add a cloud on the left edge, out to 28% across and from 8% to 30% down.
  4. Add a smaller one from 37% to 62% across and 18% to 30% down, above the glow. Keep each flat along the bottom, bumpy on top.
  5. With the brush's side, add thin coral streaks low on both sides, 30% to 37% down.
  6. Done: flat coral clouds with blue showing between them at the top.
Paints for this step1 paint, 1 new
  • Cloud coral new3 parts red, 2 parts white, 1 part ultramarine

Brushes

#10 round

Strokes

Small circles with the brush tip. Scrub tiny overlapping circles with the tip to fill each cloud; it leaves a soft, bumpy edge on top.

Watch out: Don't make all the clouds the same size: big masses up high, thin streaks lower down.

Watch out: New stroke? Try it a few times on scrap paper first.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 3 OF 12

Light the clouds and paint the sun

  1. Let the clouds dry.
  2. With the #8 round nearly dry, paint the table's values on each cloud, dark first: circles for dark and mid, dry brush for light.
  3. Widen the low streaks into thin Sunset orange bands, 30% to 45% down.
  4. With Sunset orange circles, grow a new cloud into the blue gap from 35% to 55% across, top edge down to 15%. Leave a few blue holes.
  5. Grow the left cloud up the same way, to near the top edge, out to 15% across.
  6. With the #6 round, dab a Sun cream sun half a grid square wide, centered 43% across, 42% down. Second coat once dry.

Brushes

#8 round#6 round

Strokes

Small circles with the brush tip. Scrub tiny overlapping circles for the shadow and the orange, following each cloud's bumpy shape.

Dry brush. Load just the tip with gold, wipe it almost clean, and brush lightly along the cloud bottoms so it stays feathery and see-through.

Dabbing. Tap the round tip straight down to fill the sun's small circle, keeping its edge round.

Watch out: Don't cover all the coral: the darker middle is what makes the clouds look round.

Watch out: Too much paint on the brush makes solid patches instead of soft dry brush; wipe it nearly dry.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 4 OF 12

Paint the far mountains

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the 1/2 inch flat's edge and creamy Mountain purple, cut the left ridge: peak about 12% across and a third down, sloping toward the sun.
  3. Cut a right range peaking just right of center, and a lower range to the right edge. Fill all of them down to halfway with side-to-side strokes.
  4. While wet, blend a band of Haze lilac along the mountain bases.
  5. Done: soft, plain purple mountains, lilac haze below, orange sky still showing down to the line.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Fill each range with side-to-side strokes, and stroke back over the purple-to-lilac join while wet so it blends softly.

Watch out: Don't add detail or dark lines to the mountains: far things stay soft and pale.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 5 OF 12

Paint the valley fields and the golden hill

  1. Let the mountains dry.
  2. With the 1/2 inch flat, paint the valley left of the hill in side-to-side strokes from 48% down to the line, lighter at the back as in the table. Leave a strip of haze above it.
  3. Paint the hill with Hill gold in curved strokes up the slope: its top edge rises from the line at 35% across to the right edge at 44% down. Fill to the line.
  4. While wet, blend Glow gold along the hilltop.
  5. Done: green valley left, golden hill rising right, white canvas below the line.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat

Strokes

Long horizontal blend. Lay the valley fields in side-to-side strokes, the lighter green at the back and the darker in front, stroking back over the join while wet.

Curved strokes that follow a form. Sweep the flat along the hill's slope, bottom left to top right, so the marks bend with the hill.

Watch out: Don't paint the hill one flat color: lighter on top and darker below is what makes it slope.

Watch out: About now the painting looks odd and unfinished. That's the ugly stage every painting goes through; keep going.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 6 OF 12

Dab in the dark tree line

  1. Let the hills dry.
  2. With an old stiff flat and nearly dry Woods green, tap overlapping dabs into a bumpy band from the left edge to 55% across: top about 53% down, bottom on the line.
  3. Dab a thinner band along the golden hill's bottom, from 50% across to the right edge, top about 56% down.
  4. Tap the light from the table on a few bush tops; leave dark below.
  5. Done: a dark, bumpy tree line with a few lit tops, white canvas below.

Brushes

old stiff flat or #8 round

Strokes

Dabbing. Tap the brush corner straight down over and over; the dots merge into bushy patches, more solid the more you tap.

Watch out: Don't dab single round blobs in a row: overlap them into one bumpy band.

Watch out: Too much paint makes solid dark patches; wipe the brush on a towel before tapping.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 7 OF 12

Paint the big tree

  1. Let the hill dry.
  2. With the #4 round and Trunk brown thinned to flow, press and lift up from the trunk's base at 84% across, 46% down: a trunk one grid square tall.
  3. Split it into two or three branches reaching up to about 26% down, where the crown goes.
  4. With the old stiff flat, dab the crown in overlapping clusters from 74% to 95% across and 22% to 45% down, dark first as in the table. Let branch show low.
  5. Once each layer dries, tap the next value from the table; each covers less.

Brushes

#4 roundold stiff flat

Strokes

Press and lift. Press the brush down at the base for a thick trunk, then lift toward the tip as you pull up and out, so each branch tapers.

Dabbing. Tap clusters of leaves with the brush corner, dark first, then lighter taps on the sun side over them.

Watch out: Don't cover all the dark green: the light taps go only on the sun side, the left.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 8 OF 12

Paint the balloon's stripes

  1. Let the sky dry.
  2. With the #6 round and thin Balloon orange, outline a circle centered 28% across and 15% wide (from 20% to 35%), its top 3% down.
  3. Narrow its bottom to a neck at 27% down, under the circle's center.
  4. Fill curved stripes from top to neck, left to right: red, blue, red, orange, blue, red, yellow, blue, orange, yellow (the Balloon colors). Rinse between colors.
  5. Edge stripes are one stroke; for wide ones, curve down each side, then fill between.
  6. Give yellow and orange a second coat once dry. Done: a round striped balloon, no basket.

  • Balloon yellow newYellow, straight from the tube

Brushes

#6 round

Strokes

Curved strokes that follow a form. Pull each stripe from the top down to the neck in one bending stroke, so the stripes wrap around the balloon.

Building from pieces. Start from a circle for the top, then add the two narrowing curves for the bottom.

Watch out: Don't paint straight stripes: they must curve, or the balloon looks flat.

Watch out: Rinse fully between colors so the yellow stays clean.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

STEP 9 OF 12

Shade the balloon and hang the basket

  1. Let the stripes dry fully.
  2. With the #6 round nearly dry, brush Sun cream lightly down the middle stripes in curved strokes so the center looks lit.
  3. With the same brush and creamy Burnt sienna, paint a short band across the neck.
  4. With the liner and Trunk brown thinned like ink, pull four ropes straight down from the neck, each a third of a grid square long (27% to 30% down).
  5. Dab a Burnt sienna square for the basket where the ropes end, as wide as the neck band. Done: a lit balloon with its basket.

Dry brush. Wipe the brush nearly dry and brush the cream lightly so it stays broken and see-through.

Liner work. Hold the liner upright and pull thin ink-like paint down in one steady stroke per rope.

Watch out: Liner paint too thick gives broken, skippy ropes: thin it to ink and reload often.

STEP 10 OF 12

Lay in the lavender rows and paths

  1. Dot the paths' meeting point at 61% across, 62% down. With the 1/2 inch flat and Path clay, pull two paths from it to the bottom edge, at 37-48% and 68-80% across.
  2. While wet, add the paths' light and dark from the table.
  3. Mark about six row lines on each side, a grid square apart where they meet the canvas edges, each pulled straight toward the dot.
  4. Fill the rows with the 1 inch flat and creamy Lavender dark, pulling toward the dot. Cover all white.
  5. Once dry, add the Row shadow line from the table with the 1/2 inch flat's edge.

Brushes

1/2 inch flat1 inch flat

Strokes

Strokes toward a vanishing point. Mark the meeting point with a dot, then pull every path edge and row straight toward it, wide at the bottom and thin near the dot. Check a few rows by holding the brush handle from the dot.

Long horizontal blend. Where the rows run nearly sideways at the far left and right, fill them with long side-to-side strokes, and blend the path colors while wet.

Watch out: Don't curve the rows or run them straight across: every row is a straight line pointing at the dot.

Watch out: Purple over white may need two coats; let the first dry.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

Why a diagram: Every row and both paths aim at one point; get that wrong and the field looks flat.

How it broke the shape down: The field drawn at its real proportions (a 100 by 26 band), the two paths from one point, then the row gaps as lines from the same point.

Checked against the picture: Paths meet at 63% across at the field's top and reach the bottom at 33-42% and 76-84%, as in the step image after the redo.

Point every path and row at one spot

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

STEP 11 OF 12

Dab the middle purple on the rows

  1. Let the dark rows dry.
  2. With the old stiff flat and fairly dry Lavender mid, tap short upward dabs along each row's top half, front rows first.
  3. Make dabs big in front, smaller and closer toward the back. Let a few spill over the path edges.
  4. On the front rows only (below 80% down), tap the light from the table on the tuft tops.
  5. Done: bushy, rounded rows with dark still showing at the bases.

Brushes

old stiff flat

Strokes

Dabbing. Tap the brush corner upward again and again along each row; the taps merge into bushy texture.

Watch out: Don't cover the whole row: the dark base is what makes each row look round.

Drying: About 10 minutes between steps (a hair dryer on low speeds it up). An hour after the last step before handling.

One lavender row, built up dab by dab

Dashed outline: what to paint in that picture. Arrows: which way to move the brush.

STEP 12 OF 12

Add the sunlit lavender tips

  1. Let the mid dabs dry.
  2. With the #8 round and nearly dry Lavender light, tap small upward dabs on the very top edge of each tuft, where the low sun behind the field catches it.
  3. Most go on the front rows, below 65% down; use fewer, smaller dabs toward the back. Light over dark may need a second tap once dry.
  4. Once the tips dry, tap Lavender dark back into a few gaps between the front tufts, below 75% down, so they stand out.
  5. Done: the finished painting. Yours will look different from the reference, and that's fine.

How Claude read your photosubject, light, layers

Before starting

Subject: A striped hot air balloon over a lavender field at sunset

Found in the image: just the picture

Done: none

Why: No bars, borders, captions, or page around it.

Beginner version

What made it too busy: Tiny separate things: yes (a village of houses, cypress trees, a lake glint). Textures of hundreds of items: yes (every lavender stalk, small bushes). Detail inside big shapes: yes (veined, fringed clouds). Parts: about 11, over the budget of 8.

Changed: Dropped the village, the cypresses, and the lake glint. Merged the clouds into four or five big soft masses, the far hills into two mountain bands, and the valley woods and small hill trees into one dark tree line. Turned the lavender into curved rows of loose dabs, darker at the base. Kept the balloon, the big tree, the sun, and the paths in place.

Why: With those changes every part is a big shape or one repeated mark, which the lesson can split into passes.

A sunset scene where the striped balloon is the focal point, but most of the canvas is sky and lavender. What matters is a glowing sky with round-looking clouds, simple far mountains, and a lavender field that reads as rows going back to one point. The hard parts for a beginner are the clouds' values, the balloon's curved stripes, and turning thousands of lavender stalks into something paintable.

Subject: A striped hot air balloon floating over a lavender field at sunset, with purple mountains, a golden hill, and one big tree.
Focal point: The striped balloon at the upper left (envelope from 20% to 36% across, 3% to 27% down).
Light: The setting sun, low in the middle of the picture (43% across, 41% down). Cloud edges facing the sun glow gold, the tree is lit on its left side, and the lavender tops catch pink-lilac light.

What it saw, back to front

  1. sky gradient (blue top to golden glow)
  2. clouds (coral base, then orange and gold lit edges) and the sun
  3. far mountains (two blue-purple ranges and a lilac haze band)
  4. valley fields and the golden hill
  5. dark tree line along the valley and the bottom of the golden hill
  6. the big tree on the hilltop
  7. the striped balloon, its basket and ropes
  8. the lavender field rows and the two paths
Why this techniquePaint along, back to front

The owner named it: /paint-lesson photos/blog/balloon-lavender.png acrylic-paint-along-beginner low.

ChosenPaint along, back to frontStart on a plain white canvas. Paint the sky first, then each part of the scene from farthest to nearest, each straight over the one behind it. Then the main subject, texture with simple brush moves, shadows, and highlights last.

A back-to-front paint-along suits a landscape with a big sky and a foreground field: sky, clouds, mountains, hills, tree, balloon, then the field in dark, mid, and light passes.

Passed onBlock in, then build up (acrylic-block-in-beginner)

Not chosen: the owner named the paint-along technique. It would also fit less well, since its sketch and tonal block-in steps suit a single object more than a sky-and-field landscape.

How the paint recipes were worked out26 paints, free

Paint doesn't mix like light on a screen: blue and yellow make green, not gray. So the recipes come from a pigment mixing model (Mixbox), not a guess. For each paint it tried every simple recipe from your tubes, up to three colors plus white, and kept the one that lands closest to the color in the painting. Delta E is how far off it lands: under 2 is hard to see, under 5 is close, and over 8 means these tubes can't quite make it.

Why the steps go in this order12 steps

Back to front, per the technique: the sky runs down to 63% so the hills go over it, then cloud base and cloud light as separate value steps, far mountains, the valley and golden hill, the tree line, the big tree, the balloon (stripes, then shine and basket), and last the lavender in three passes (flat dark rows, mid dabs, light tips) so no step jumps from flat to dense texture.

  1. 1. Blend the sunset sky

    Every later layer sits on the sky, and it's one wet blend, so it goes first and runs well past the horizon.

  2. 2. Block in the cloud shapes

    Clouds are 3D, so they get a dark base first; split from the lighting so each step is one move.

  3. 3. Light the clouds and paint the sun

    The mid and light values on the sun side make the clouds round; the sun goes on here because it's the brightest thing in the sky and sits in the glow.

  4. 4. Paint the far mountains

    Farthest land, pale and soft, over the dry sky.

  5. 5. Paint the valley fields and the golden hill

    The next distance: the valley and the golden hill, both broad fields of color.

  6. 6. Dab in the dark tree line

    The dark band of woods sits on the valley and the hill base; one dabbing move.

  7. 7. Paint the big tree

    Sits on the hilltop, in front of the sky and hill; trunk, dark crown, and gold taps.

  8. 8. Paint the balloon's stripes

    The focal point, painted once the sky around it is done; stripes as one curved-stroke move.

  9. 9. Shade the balloon and hang the basket

    Shine and the small details go on the dry stripes, liner work last for the balloon.

  10. 10. Lay in the lavender rows and paths

    The foreground goes last over everything; flat dark rows and paths first.

  11. 11. Dab the middle purple on the rows

    Second pass of the field texture: one dab size, mid value.

  12. 12. Add the sunlit lavender tips

    The brightest highlights, last, ending at the finished painting.

Filters it tried7 free looks
Where Claude drew diagrams4 steps, free

Four steps needed a diagram: the balloon (a shaped object that appears whole), the tree (a trunk that forks), the lavender rows (placement depends on perspective), and the mid lavender dabs (a repeated mark the step reviewer asked to see built up). Skies, clouds, mountains, fields, and highlights are blends or one repeated mark the words cover.

  • Step 7: Paint the big tree beginner check

    Noticed: Where the trunk forks and where the gold goes aren't clear from the picture alone.

    Pieces: A Y trunk first, then the crown as one wide oval with clusters around its edge, then gold taps only on the left and top.

  • Step 8: Paint the balloon's stripes beginner check

    Noticed: The balloon appears whole in one step, and its stripes have to curve with the shape or it looks flat.

    Pieces: A circle for the top, then two curves narrowing to the neck, then the stripes as curved lines from top to neck, bending more toward the edges.

  • Step 10: Lay in the lavender rows and paths beginner check

    Noticed: Every row and both paths aim at one point; get that wrong and the field looks flat.

    Pieces: The field drawn at its real proportions (a 100 by 26 band), the two paths from one point, then the row gaps as lines from the same point.

  • Step 11: Dab the middle purple on the rows step review (6b)

    Noticed: The step reviewer (6b) asked to see one row built up tap by tap, since the dabs repeat across the whole field.

    Pieces: One dark row, then a few upward taps along its top, then more taps filling the top half with the dark left below.

Looked at and left without one

  • Step 1: A blended gradient; the words give where each color goes.
  • Step 2: One repeated mark (small circles) in simple masses; the reviewer proposed a diagram, but the words and the step image show the flat-bottom, bumpy-top shape well enough.
  • Step 3: The reviewer proposed a three-panel cloud diagram; the text now names dark, mid, and light and where each goes, and the before and after pictures show it. Kept to save diagrams for shapes.
  • Step 4: Simple flat silhouettes against the sky.
  • Step 5: Broad fields of color in curved and horizontal strokes.
  • Step 6: A repeated dabbing mark in a band; the reviewer proposed a diagram, but it's the same tap as the tree crown, which has one.
  • Step 9: Small details (a band, four lines, a square) the words place exactly.
  • Step 12: Small taps on the tops of rows already built in the lavender-mid diagram.

What Claude would do differentlyfor the next lesson
  • The research and YAML have no stroke_results entry for strokes that follow a path or a row toward a vanishing point, or for plain horizontal strokes on fields; the step reviewer flagged both as uncovered. Worth adding to stroke_results.
  • The research covers clouds, hills, fields, trees, and balloons, but not perspective in rows (lavender, crops, vineyards): where rows and paths converge and how to keep them aimed at one point. I relied on general practice there.
  • Skill/tool quirk: mix solved the 'Burnt sienna' paint (planned as the tube straight) as 2 red + 2 ultramarine + 1 burnt sienna, Delta E 0.7, so the page shows a three-tube recipe for a tube color. The step reviewer caught the confusion. mix should keep a paint that is a single palette tube as that tube.
  • Step renders still drift: clouds and the tree line change shape between almost every step (6b found drift in 11 of 12 steps), though the round-2 image review passed them. The image review checklist tolerates it as brushwork; the step review doesn't.
  • The first round of step renders stopped the sky at 50-59% even with a measured straight edge at 63% in looks_like; one redo each fixed it. Saying the edge in the fix as 'all the way down to' worked better than in the plan.
  • Lavender mid and Lavender light land at Delta E about 7.5 from the finish with these five tubes: the picture's saturated violet needs a purer purple than ultramarine plus cadmium red gives.
  • preview-diagrams reads lesson.json, so it reports 0 diagrams (and 'no Chrome or Edge found', which is misleading) until publish has run after construct specs are added. The skill's step 7 could say to republish before previewing.
